lines.text: In twenty twenty five, a research paper gave the world a number. Cache augmented generation was forty times faster than RAG. The number is real. The comparison is not.
You have probably seen the headline. CAG is forty times faster than RAG, retrieval free, and more accurate too.
Search that claim and you will find it repeated on LinkedIn, in engineering blogs, and in presentation slides. Almost nobody opens the paper.
So we did. We downloaded both versions of the source, opened the tables, and read the names of the baseline rows.
What we found is better than a misquote. The paper changed the label, and the internet kept quoting the old one.
This is the story of a number that survived because it was repeated, not because it was read.
First, what the two systems actually do.
RAG stands for retrieval augmented generation. Split documents into chunks, embed them into an index, and fetch the few most relevant chunks for each question.
The model sees those chunks and the question. It never sees the whole knowledge base. Its answer can only be as good as the chunks that were fetched.
CAG takes the opposite bet. Cache augmented generation preloads the entire curated corpus into the context window once.
The model reads it, computes the key and value tensors for every token, and saves that state. The saved state is the KV cache.
When a question arrives, only the question is processed. The corpus is already there. No retrieval step, no embedding lookup, no ranking.
After the answer, the extra question tokens are trimmed and the cache returns to its clean state.
That is a clever idea. It removes a whole class of failures: the right document never being retrieved at all.
But notice what the cache does not remove. The model still attends over every token in that corpus for every token it generates.
The cache saves the reading. It does not save the thinking.
So how was the forty times figure produced? The authors tested Llama three point one, eight billion parameters, on two question answering benchmarks.
SQuAD, where the answer sits in one passage, and HotPotQA, where you must connect facts across documents.
They built three corpus sizes. Sixteen, thirty two, and sixty four documents, from twenty one thousand up to eighty five thousand tokens.
The largest set is the interesting one. Sixty four documents, eighty five thousand tokens, and one thousand three hundred forty four questions.
They ran sparse BM25 retrieval, dense vector retrieval, plain long context with no cache, and their cached method.
Every system used the same model. The hardware was eight Tesla V100 GPUs.
Now open table three, the response time table, and read the names of the rows carefully.
Here is the number everyone quotes. Re-reading the whole corpus for every question takes ninety two point zero eight seconds.
With the cache precomputed, the same question takes two point two six seconds.
Ninety two divided by two point two six is forty point seven. That is where forty times comes from.
But look at the name of the ninety two second row. In the published version it says in context learning. In the earlier version, it said without CAG.
It is not RAG. It is the model reading the entire corpus again from scratch, on every single question.
Now look at the row that actually says RAG. Sparse retrieval, top three passages: zero point zero zero zero eight seconds to retrieve, and zero point six six six seven to generate.
Under one second. The cached method takes two point two six.
On the paper's own largest test set, plain keyword RAG was three point four times faster than CAG.
The forty times speedup is real. It just compares against the slowest possible baseline, not against RAG.
What about accuracy? This is where the story gets stranger.
The published table two gives CAG a BERT score of zero point seven four zero seven on the large Hot Pot Q A set.
Sparse RAG with five passages scores zero point seven five three five. RAG wins that row.
But the earlier arXiv version scored CAG at zero point seven five two seven, and marked it as the best result.
Same authors, same experiment, two different tables. We checked the source files.
In version two, the old table is still in the Latex. It is wrapped in an if false block, so it never appears in the published PDF.
The authors also changed the baseline label from without CAG to in context learning, and replaced the old numbers.
Articles published after that revision kept quoting the first version. Some still claim CAG was more accurate in every configuration.
The honest conclusion is narrower. CAG led on the small and medium sets. On the largest one, the result depends on which version you read.
There is a second cost nobody puts in the headline. The cache has to live somewhere.
Llama three point one eight billion has thirty two layers, eight key value heads, and one hundred twenty eight dimensions per head.
One token needs two values per head, in two byte precision. That is about one hundred twenty eight kilobytes per token.
Across eighty five thousand tokens, that is roughly eleven gigabytes of cache, before framework overhead.
That is our arithmetic, from the model's published shape, not a figure from the paper.
The model weights themselves are about sixteen gigabytes. The cached corpus is most of another model.
So is CAG useless? No. It solves a real problem, in a narrow setting.
If your knowledge base is small, stable, queried constantly, and does not need different permissions for different people, preloading and caching is a clean design.
Internal handbooks, frequently asked questions, support playbooks. The paper names those exact use cases.
The authors state the boundary themselves. The method becomes impractical for significantly larger datasets.
And they suggest the hybrid. Preload a foundation context, then retrieve only for the edge cases.
A recent independent test pushed this to six hundred twenty thousand tokens. CAG stayed accurate, but time to first token rose to about fifteen seconds. Retrieval stayed near one.
So the rule of thumb is not which technique wins. It is how much text you are willing to hold in memory for every answer.
The paper's own title says, don't do RAG. Its own limitations say when not to do CAG.
The next time someone tells you a system is forty times faster, ask what the other row is called.
The number was never the lie. The label next to it was.
Source: Chan, Chen, Cheng and Huang. "Don't Do RAG". The Web Conference twenty twenty five, companion proceedings.
We read both versions so you do not have to.
Read the table.
